To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
veterans with Gulf War Illness show a hyperarousal to emotional distractors, and that this is associated with a disruption of cholinergic, dopamine, and/or white matter systems.

Gulf War Illness syndrome groups have different patterns of ERP response to auditory distractor stimuli, which may reflect cholinergic gating, dopaminergic inhibitory control, and white matter integrity.
the three Gulf War Illness Syndromes (GWISs) 1-3 have different ERP profiles that are consistent with their reported hyperarousal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurobiological basis for the hyperarousal symptom in the syndromes, and our findings are compatible with a model in which hyperarousal is a symptom of multiple neurophysiologic dysfunctions.
identifying the neural substrates underlying Gulf War syndrome and other stress-related disorders.
understanding the neural basis of hyperarousability, which has been reported by veterans of both the 1991 and 2003 Persian Gulf Wars.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ERP data suggest that Gulf War illness syndrome 2 and 1 are associated with compromised cholinergic gating in the reticulothalamic system and that Gulf War illness syndromes 1, 2, and 3 are associated with compromised dopaminergic gating in the basal ganglia and that all three syndromes are associated with compromised white matter integrity.

the ERP data are consistent with the hypothesis that Gulf War illness is a neurobiological syndrome that may be associated with cholinergic, dopamine, and white matter damage, but that the precise nature of these deficits remains unclear.

the hyperarousability of the Gulf War veterans, as reflected in the ERP data, is associated with a combination of damage to cholinergically and dopaminergically mediated brainstem, basal ganglia, and frontal lobe systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hyperarousal is a common feature of Gulf War Illness, with different underlying mechanisms.
the hyperarousability of the ill veterans, which is a core symptom of the syndrome, is related to the disruption of multiple brain systems.
hyperarousal is associated with cholinergic and dopamine dysfunctions and white matter damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
different patterns of brain dysfunction can account for different aspects of Gulf War illness symptoms.
different patterns of brain activity may be related to different aspects of the hyperarousal symptoms.
the three syndrome groups have unique ERP profiles that can be explained by different underlying pathologies.
